pages.text_content: Chef Cat wore a tiny white hat and an apron splattered with tomato sauce. Every morning she padded into her kitchen, whiskers twitching at the glorious smells. Today was extra special — she was teaching her friends to cook for the very first time. She stirred her big bubbling pot and called out, 'Come in, come in! The kitchen is warm and the adventure is about to begin!'

First came Rabbit, hopping in with a basket of bright orange carrots. Then Mouse arrived, so small she needed a stool to reach the counter. Finally Bear stomped in, wearing an apron three sizes too small. Chef Cat smiled at each of them. 'Today we make carrot soup,' she announced, 'and everyone has an important job!' Rabbit chopped, Mouse measured the spices with tiny careful paws, and Bear stirred the great big pot round and round.

Then disaster struck! Bear stirred too enthusiastically and soup splashed everywhere. Mouse squeaked. Rabbit gasped. Bear's ears drooped sadly. But Chef Cat simply laughed and reached for a cloth. 'Every cook spills something,' she said. 'The secret is to keep going.' They cleaned up together and tasted the soup. It was warm and sweet and absolutely perfect. 'Can we cook again tomorrow?' Bear asked hopefully. Chef Cat refilled every bowl. 'In this kitchen,' she purred, 'there is always more to make — and always more to share.' THE END

Out in the sparkling blue sea sat a little island where only one child lived. Her name was Isla, and she had tall coconut trees, a sandy beach, and a cosy hut — but no friends. Each evening she sat on the shore watching the sunset, wishing someone might sail her way. She had drawn pictures of imaginary friends and named them all, but drawings cannot laugh or play or share your coconut cake.

One morning Isla spotted a bottle bobbing in the waves. Inside was a note: 'Hello! I am Leo. I live on the island to the east. I am also lonely. Would you like to be friends?' Isla's heart leapt. She wrote back immediately, tucked the note in the bottle, and threw it as far as she could. Letters flew back and forth. Isla learned Leo loved drawing maps and had a pet crab named Pinchy. Leo learned Isla could climb any tree and always talked to the seagulls.

Though they had never met, they already felt like the best of friends. Then one day Leo's letter said: 'I am building a raft. I am coming to visit.' Isla spent three days making coconut cake and practising what she would say. When Leo's raft bumped onto her beach, they both stood staring for a moment — then burst out laughing at exactly the same time. It turned out friends who write wonderful letters make even more wonderful real ones. THE END

Every year the biggest event in the galaxy was the Star Trail Race — a wild zoom through asteroid fields, past glowing nebulas, and around the rings of Saturn. This year eleven-year-old Zara was finally old enough to enter. Her ship, the Silver Spark, was small and a bit dented, but Zara had tuned the engine herself. 'Speed isn't everything,' her dad always said. 'Smart flying wins races.' Zara had written that on a sticker above her controls.

At the starting line Zara looked at her rivals. Blaze had an enormous red rocket. Rex had twin turbo boosters. The twins Mia and Moa flew in perfect gleaming formation. Everyone assumed Zara would come last. The countdown began. Three, two, one, ZOOM! Ships exploded across the sky in every direction. Blaze shot ahead immediately. But Zara went smart — tight corners through the asteroid field, speed boosts caught from passing comets, fuel saved for the final straight.

One by one the other racers hit trouble. Blaze got tangled in a meteor shower. Rex's boosters sputtered out. The twins took a wrong turn past Jupiter and ended up going backwards. Zara flew steady and sure, the Silver Spark humming perfectly. She crossed the finish line first, her little ship glowing like a real star. The crowd went wild. Zara floated out of the cockpit and whispered the words on her sticker: 'Smart flying wins races.' THE END

Mara had never seen the ocean before. When her family arrived at the seaside, she stood at the water's edge with her toes in the cold foam and her mouth wide open. The sea stretched so far she could not see where it ended. It was enormous and blue-green and alive. 'Go on,' said her mum. 'It won't bite.' Mara took one step forward, then another. A wave rushed up and tickled her ankles and she laughed so hard her belly ached.

With her little net and bucket, Mara explored the rock pools. Inside each one was a tiny world — spiky sea urchins, scuttling hermit crabs, rippling anemones that looked exactly like flowers. A small orange starfish sat perfectly still on a rock. 'Hello,' Mara whispered. She felt certain it winked at her. She did not pick it up. Some creatures, her dad told her, are happiest exactly where they are. Mara decided that was very wise advice for people too.

As the sun dipped low and turned the sea to gold, Mara sat on the sand with a bucket full of shells. She held each one to her ear. Her grandmother had told her you could hear the ocean inside a shell — and it was true. A deep rushing swirling sound, like the sea whispering something wonderful. Mara decided she would come back to the ocean every single year for the rest of her life. There was simply far too much wonder to see it all in one day. THE END

Princess Rowan was not the sort of princess who sat around waiting to be rescued. She preferred muddy boots, tangled hair, and a good adventure. One morning she slipped out of the palace before breakfast and headed for the Enchanted Forest — the one place everyone told her never to go. The moment she stepped between the trees, the whole forest shimmered gold, as if it had been waiting for her for a very long time.

Strange and wonderful things happened in the Enchanted Forest. Flowers whispered her name. A fox with silver fur led her down a path that had not existed a moment before. At the end of the path sat an ancient tree with a hollow trunk, and inside the hollow was a tiny door no bigger than Rowan's hand. A voice said, 'Only someone truly brave and truly kind can open this door.' Rowan thought carefully. Then she knocked very gently and said, 'Please may I come in? I would love to meet you.'

The door swung open to reveal a whole village of tiny woodland sprites, no taller than her thumb, trapped inside the tree for a hundred years by a forgetful enchantment. No one had ever thought to knock politely before. Rowan carefully helped them out one by one into the warm sunlight. The sprites cheered. The forest sang. The silver fox bowed deeply. Rowan walked home through golden trees, muddy boots and all, knowing that sometimes the greatest magic is simply being kind. THE END

Max loved dinosaurs more than anything in the world. His room was packed with books, models, and drawings of every species he knew. So when he discovered a strange machine in his grandfather's garage — covered in dials and levers and a sign reading TIME MACHINE — he knew exactly where he wanted to go. He set the dial to 66 million years ago, took a very deep breath, and pulled the lever.

WHOOOOSH! The machine rattled and shook and flashed with light. When it stopped, Max stepped outside into a world he had only ever seen in books. Enormous ferns stretched to the sky. The ground trembled with heavy footsteps. And there, right in front of him, was a real breathing Triceratops — three enormous horns gleaming in the prehistoric sun. Max stood completely still. The Triceratops tilted its gigantic head and sniffed at him curiously.

Max spent the most incredible day of his life watching dinosaurs — Brachiosaurus munching treetops, Velociraptors chasing lizards, and a baby Stegosaurus that followed him everywhere like a very large very spiky puppy. When it was time to leave, Max patted the baby Stegosaurus gently on its nose. 'I will never forget you,' he whispered. Back in his grandfather's garage, Max sat down and started drawing every single thing he had seen. No book could ever be as good as having actually been there. THE END

Everyone in the neighbourhood said the old treehouse at the end of Bramble Lane was haunted. Lights flickered in it at night. Strange sounds drifted from it on quiet evenings. No child had dared go near it in years — everyone except Priya. She watched it from her bedroom window every morning and thought: I am going in there. One October afternoon she marched across the garden, climbed the rope ladder, and pushed open the creaky wooden door.

The treehouse was dark and dusty, stuffed with old comic books, a broken telescope, and impressive cobwebs. Then a sound! A rustling in the corner! A flash of pale blue light! Priya squeezed her eyes shut — and then opened them. Sitting in the corner was a small ghost, no bigger than a football, glowing faintly and looking extremely embarrassed. 'I wasn't trying to scare anyone,' the ghost said in a tiny voice. 'I just didn't know where else to go.'

His name was Pip. He had lived in the treehouse for fifty years, ever since the boy who built it had grown up and gone away. Priya looked around at the dusty comics and the broken telescope and had an idea. 'I'll fix it up,' she said. 'And you can stay. We'll share it.' Pip glowed so brightly the whole tree lit up. Together they cleaned, fixed the telescope, and spent every afternoon reading comics and watching the stars. The treehouse was not haunted at all. It was just lonely — and loneliness, Priya discovered, is easily cured. THE END

Cog was a robot who lived in a workshop at the edge of town. He had been built to sort nuts and bolts, and he was very good at it. But sorting nuts and bolts is quite a lonely job, and what Cog wanted more than anything was a friend. Through the workshop window he watched children walking past — laughing, chatting, chasing each other — and he wished with all his circuits that he knew how to do any of those things.

One day a girl named Bea pressed her nose flat against the workshop window. 'Hello in there!' she called. Cog froze — no one had ever spoken to him before. Very slowly, he lifted one metal hand and gave a small careful wave. Bea's face broke into a huge grin. 'Do you want to come out and play?' Cog looked at his pile of unsorted bolts, then at Bea's friendly face. He put down the bolt he was holding, walked to the door, and opened it for the very first time.

Bea taught Cog hopscotch — though he was rather heavy and left dents in the pavement, which made them both laugh. Cog taught Bea to sort bolts by size, which she found surprisingly satisfying. They discovered Cog was excellent at remembering jokes, and Bea was brilliant at explaining feelings, which Cog found extremely useful. By the end of the afternoon, Cog had learned the most important thing no one had ever programmed into him: making a friend is as simple as opening the door. THE END

On the first day at Heroic Heights School, every student received a cape. Some were red, some blue, some gleaming gold. But Nadia's cape was grey — the only grey one in the whole class. 'Grey means your power is unknown,' said the teacher, Ms Marvel. 'Some of the greatest heroes started grey.' Nadia tried hard not to feel disappointed. Around her, other students were already floating, sparking, and turning invisible. Nadia stood quietly in her grey cape, waiting.

In Power Development class, Nadia tried everything. She could not fly. She could not blast things. When she tried to turn invisible she went slightly transparent, which was not quite the same. Then the teacher set a challenge: get the kitten down from the very tall tree. The other students tried their powers and failed spectacularly. Nadia looked at the kitten. She looked at the tree. She thought carefully. Then she went to the canteen, found a tin of sardines, opened it, and held it up. The kitten climbed down immediately.

Ms Marvel smiled the biggest smile any of them had ever seen. 'And what power is THAT?' she asked the class. 'Problem solving,' said one student, impressed. 'Thinking before acting,' said another. Nadia's grey cape began to shimmer — and turned the most brilliant dazzling silver anyone at Heroic Heights had ever seen. The rarest superpower of all, Ms Marvel told them, was not strength or speed or flight. It was the ability to stop, think, and find the cleverest solution. And Nadia had it in abundance. THE END
